how-much-concrete-for-a-driveway.html.text:
CONCRETE YARDAGE

How much concrete for a driveway?

Concrete is sold by the cubic yard, not by the square foot. A 20×40 driveway at 4 inches and the same pad at 6 inches for an RV look identical on a lot sketch and differ by half the material on the ticket. Thickness is the number a “$8 a square foot” quote drops.

Yards the plant will bill —

The conversion

Cubic yards = length (ft) × width (ft) × thickness (in) ÷ 12 ÷ 27. One cubic yard is 27 cubic feet. Add waste for over-excavate and spillage — 5–10% is a common starting range, not a rule — then expect the plant to bill the next quarter yard. That rounded-up ticket is what you pay, even if the slab only needed 9.88 yards on paper.

Worked 20×40 examples

At 4 inches: 20 × 40 × 4 ÷ 12 ÷ 27 = 9.88 yards before waste. With 8% waste that is 10.67 yards, billed as 10.75 yards.

At 6 inches: the same driveway is 14.81 yards before waste. Same forms, same square footage, 50% more concrete. If you quoted the 4-inch square-foot price on a 6-inch spec, the extra yards come out of your pocket.

What square-foot quotes miss

  • Forms are priced by linear feet of edge, not by area. A long skinny walk has more form per yard than a square patio.
  • Finish labor: stamped and exposed aggregate take two to three times the hours of a broom driveway.
  • Access: a pump is a few hundred dollars; a wheelbarrow run is hours.
  • Short-load fees: many plants add one under about five yards, which is why a small stoop is rarely “cheap per square foot.”

To turn yardage into a bid — forms, finish, access, demo, burden, and the walk-away price — use the concrete bid calculator.

Common questions

How many cubic yards of concrete for a 20x40 driveway?

A 20 by 40 foot driveway at 4 inches is 9.88 cubic yards before waste. With a typical 8% waste factor the plant will usually bill 10.75 yards after rounding up to a quarter yard. The same pad at 6 inches is 14.81 yards before waste.

How do you convert square feet and inches into cubic yards?

Cubic yards = length in feet × width in feet × thickness in inches ÷ 12 ÷ 27. One cubic yard is 27 cubic feet. Thickness is the term a square-foot rule of thumb drops, and it is the one that changes the ticket.

Why is a square-foot driveway quote often wrong?

Concrete is sold by the cubic yard. Two driveways of the same area that differ by two inches of thickness differ by 50% in material. Forms are priced by linear feet of edge, stamped finish takes more labor than broom, and many plants add a short-load fee under about five yards.

No warranty. This free page is not engineering, structural, or business advice. Confirm mix, thickness, and reinforcement with a qualified professional and the ready-mix plant before you order. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

FOR CONCRETE CONTRACTORS

Bid the yards and the forms, not the square footage.

Price a driveway, patio, or slab the way the trade actually does: area times thickness for cubic yards, waste and the plant’s quarter-yard ticket, forms by the edge, finish by the surface, and a separate line for chute vs wheelbarrow vs pump. You get the bid, what it works out to per yard and per square foot, and the number below which the pour loses money.

The pour

One row per slab. Thickness is what turns a cheap square-foot quote into a losing job — a 6-inch RV pad is 50% more concrete than a 4-inch driveway of the same size. Pick a finish to start from a common labor figure, then replace it with a time from your own crew.

Material, access, and demo

Most plants add a short-load fee under about five yards. A 5×5 stoop that looked cheap per square foot often loses the job on that fee plus the truck minimum.

Hand the customer a proposal

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Where the yards go

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting finish hours are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a benchmark, or a guarantee — time your own crews and replace them. Confirm slump, mix, and reinforcement with the engineer or the ready-mix plant before you order.

    Common questions

    What does this concrete estimate include?

    Each slab’s cubic yards from its area and thickness, a waste percentage rounded up to the plant’s billed order increment, forms priced by perimeter, reinforcement priced by area, finish labor by the finish you pick, access costs for a pump or wheelbarrow pour, a short-load fee if the order falls under your threshold, demo and haul of any existing slab, and overhead and margin on top.

    Why does the ordered yardage differ from the raw calculated volume?

    Ready-mix plants typically bill in quarter-yard increments, so after your waste percentage is added the tool rounds the order up to the next one. The exact volume and the ordered volume are shown separately so you can see what you’ll actually be billed for, rather than eating the rounding difference yourself.

    What is the “80-lb bags (comparison only)” number for, if the bid prices ready-mix?

    It is not part of the priced bid — it converts your ordered cubic yards (waste included) into 80-lb bags at about 0.6 cubic feet per bag, so you can weigh a hardware-store bag run against calling in a ready-mix truck. Once a pour is over about a cubic yard, bagging it is almost never the cheaper path; the bag count exists mainly to confirm that a small patch, footing, or post base is one of the rare jobs where it might be worth comparing.

    Does finish labor account for a stamped or exposed-aggregate patio the same as a broom driveway?

    No. Finish hours per 100 square feet are different for broom, smooth trowel, exposed aggregate, and stamped finishes, and a stamped or decorative finish carries meaningfully more hours than a broom finish of the same size. Pick the preset that matches the job, or replace it with your own crew’s times.

    Does this check the mix design, slump, or reinforcement spec?

    No. Reinforcement is priced only as a flat cost per square foot for wire mesh or rebar, and there is no mix design, slump, or engineering check built in. Confirm those specifics with your ready-mix plant or an engineer before you pour.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your entries are optionally kept in this browser’s local storage as a draft so a reload doesn’t lose them, and nothing is sent to a server. A share link encodes only the job details you see on screen into the web address itself, so copying one and sending it does not upload anything either.

    What’s the difference between the total cost and the price shown?

    Total cost is concrete, forms, reinforcement, labor, demo, and access fees plus overhead — the walk-away number. The price on top applies your target margin, so it is what you’d need to charge to hit that margin rather than just cover your costs.

vs-a-flat-price-per-square-foot.html.text:
← Concrete Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat price per square foot

Homeowners and GCs ask for a price per square foot. Concrete is sold by the cubic yard — and thickness, finish, forms, and access all change what a pour costs at the exact same square footage.

What a flat price per square foot is

A price per square foot is the fastest number to quote over the phone or text: multiply the footprint by a rate, read back a total. It is also the unit customers already think in, because it is how the rest of home improvement is priced.

The rate behind it was learned from a specific pour — a given thickness, a given finish, a given access method — and then reused for the next square footage that comes in, whether or not that next pour shares any of those.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each slab's length, width, and thickness (or a square-footage override), a waste percentage, your ready-mix price per yard, form cost per linear foot, finish preset or your own hours, reinforcement, access method, and a short-load fee, plus your own wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin. It converts area and thickness into cubic yards the way a plant bills them, prices forms by the edge and finish by the surface, and returns the price, the price per square foot, the price per cubic yard, and the effective hourly rate — for this pour, not a rate carried over from the last one.

What a flat price per square foot doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate for a 4-inch driveway and a 6-inch RV pad on the identical footprint, even though the thicker pour needs 50% more concrete. Computes cubic yards from area × thickness for every slab, rounded up to the quarter-yard the plant actually bills, so a thicker pour orders and costs more without anyone eyeballing a markup.
Has no line for the finish — a broom driveway and a stamped patio of the same size get the same rate, even though stamped work takes two to three times the labor. Starts finish labor from a broom, trowel, exposed, or stamped preset in crew-hours per 100 square feet, editable to the contractor's own crew.
Prices forms, if at all, as part of the blended square-foot rate, so an odd-shaped pour with more edge per square foot costs the same as a plain rectangle. Prices forms by the linear foot of perimeter, computed from the tape-measure dimensions, as its own line separate from the slab area.
Has no separate line for access — a pump job and a wheelbarrow run down a long yard get the same square-foot rate. Prices chute, wheelbarrow, or pump as their own access line, including the pump's flat fee and the extra labor hours a wheelbarrow run adds.
Gives the customer a number to compare against a competitor's postcard rate, not a number to check a quote against. Reports price per square foot, price per cubic yard, and effective hourly rate alongside the price, so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before you match it.

Same 800 square feet, two different pours

Using this calculator's own shipped starting inputs — 8% waste, $175 ready-mix, $3.50 per linear foot of form, broom finish, truck-chute access, $28 blended wage, 30% burden, 12% overhead, 20% target margin:

A 20×40 driveway (800 square feet) poured 4 inches thick orders 10.75 cubic yards and prices at $4,679.88 — $5.85 per square foot.

Pour the identical 800-square-foot footprint 6 inches thick instead, for an RV pad — same finish, same access, same everything else — and it orders 16 cubic yards, costs $4,772.90 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $5,966.13 — $7.46 per square foot. Quoting the 6-inch pour at the 4-inch pour's learned rate of $5.85 per square foot reproduces the 4-inch price, $4,679.88, which is $93.02 below the 6-inch pour's own break-even cost — before counting the $1,286.25 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 20% target margin. Same 800 square feet, same rate, one pour that pays and one that loses money the moment the thickness changes.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per square foot get a concrete pour wrong?

Because concrete is sold by the cubic yard, not the square foot, and square footage alone does not say how many yards a pour needs. A 20x40 driveway poured 4 inches thick is 800 square feet and about 9.88 raw cubic yards. The identical 800-square-foot footprint poured 6 inches thick for an RV needs about 14.81 raw cubic yards -- 50% more material on the same sketch. A price learned per square foot from the 4-inch pour prices the 6-inch pour as if it used the same concrete, because square footage cannot tell a 4-inch slab from a 6-inch one.

What else does square footage alone miss?

Finish, forms, and access. A broom finish takes about 0.85 crew-hours per 100 square feet; a stamped or decorative finish takes roughly two to three times that on the identical area. Forms are priced by the linear foot of edge, not the square footage inside it, so an oddly shaped pour with more perimeter per square foot costs more in forms than a simple rectangle of the same area. Access -- a truck chute, a wheelbarrow run, or a pump -- is its own labor and fee line that a per-square-foot number has no place to put. None of these show up in square footage.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped starting inputs: a 20x40 driveway poured 4 inches thick, broom finish, orders 10.75 cubic yards and prices at $4,679.88 -- $5.85 per square foot. Pour the identical 800-square-foot footprint 6 inches thick instead, same finish, same access, and it orders 16 cubic yards, costs $4,772.90 to run before profit, and this calculator prices it at $5,966.13 -- $7.46 per square foot. Quoting the 6-inch pour at the 4-inch pour's learned rate of $5.85 per square foot reproduces the 4-inch price, $4,679.88, which is $93.02 below the 6-inch pour's own break-even cost and $1,286.25 short of what this calculator says the job should charge at a 20% target margin.

Is a flat price per square foot ever a reasonable shorthand?

As a rough, same-thickness, same-finish comparison across similar pours, a per-square-foot number can be a useful sanity check -- it is what this calculator itself reports alongside the price. The risk is using it to quote sight unseen across different thicknesses, finishes, or access methods, because the rate learned from one pour does not carry over to a pour that differs on any of those, and by the time someone is standing on site to notice, the square-foot number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local ready-mix prices or labor rates?

No. It has no data on your local plant's per-yard price, your form lumber supplier, or your crew's wage. It takes each slab's dimensions and thickness, your waste percentage, your ready-mix price, form cost, finish hours, reinforcement, access method, and short-load fee, and your own wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into cubic yards, labor hours, and a price for this pour -- the arithmetic a flat square-foot number skips, not a market survey.

Open the Concrete Bid Calculator to price your own pour, or read how much concrete a driveway needs.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, financial, engineering, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. It is not a structural design, a mix design, or a code check. Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, ready-mix tickets, and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device, and this page makes no live comparison against any competing service — it is a static page describing the calculator's own worked example.

vs-stack.html.text:
← Concrete Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. STACK

Two different shapes: STACK is an account-based takeoff and estimating platform for running a contractor's whole preconstruction workflow, across trades and across many jobs. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this driveway, patio, or slab cost, before you offer it to the customer.

What each tool is for

STACK is a cloud-based construction takeoff and estimating platform used by contractors across trades — including concrete, but also framing, roofing, electrical, and general contracting — to turn digital plans into a measured takeoff, build estimates and proposals from it, and manage the broader preconstruction workflow, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every project. STACK's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that takeoff and estimating software describe measuring plan sets and building estimates from them across a portfolio of jobs and trades; none describe working out what one concrete pour should cost from its own area, thickness, forms, and finish labor before you quote it — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what STACK does. It does not read a plan set, manage a takeoff library, or track a bid across a sales pipeline. It takes one slab's area and thickness for cubic yards, a waste percentage rounded up to the ready-mix plant's billed order increment, form footage, reinforcement, finish labor by the surface you pick, access cost for a pump or wheelbarrow pour, a short-load fee if the order falls under your threshold, and demo and haul of any existing slab, and turns that into the recommended price, the walk-away number, the price per cubic yard, the price per square foot, and a check of whether a price you're already considering still clears your own margin — plus a printable customer proposal. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I need to run digitized takeoffs from plan sets and manage estimates across many projects and trades.STACK, or a comparable takeoff platform — running that ongoing workflow is not something this calculator does.
What should I charge for this driveway, patio, or slab, given its area, thickness, forms, finish, and access?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
Why does the cubic yardage I'm billed for differ from the raw calculated volume?This calculator's waste percentage and quarter-yard order rounding, shown separately from the exact volume.
A customer's budget is below what I'd normally quote. Does it still clear my walk-away number?This calculator's proposed-price check — it flags a price below break-even before you agree to it.
I already have jobs estimated and need to manage takeoffs, bids, and proposals across an ongoing pipeline.STACK — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
How does the yardage-and-forms math behind a concrete price actually work?This calculator's own driveway yardage walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. STACK's tools are used through a paid account.

Most concrete and general contractors get different value from each: STACK (or a comparable takeoff platform) for measuring plans and running estimates across an ongoing pipeline of projects and trades as an account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what a single pour should cost before it is offered. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a signed proposal, an invoice, or a structural or mix-design check.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or STACK?

They do different jobs, and a concrete or general contractor of any size will likely end up touching both. STACK is a cloud-based construction takeoff and estimating platform used by contractors across trades to digitize plans into a takeoff, generate estimates and proposals, and manage the broader preconstruction workflow, on an ongoing paid account. This calculator does one narrower thing: it takes a slab's area, thickness, and waste percentage to get ordered cubic yards, plus form footage, reinforcement, finish labor by surface, access for a pump or wheelbarrow, a short-load fee, and demo and haul of an existing slab, and turns that into the recommended price, the walk-away number, price per cubic yard, and price per square foot, before you have quoted anything. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A contractor already running digitized takeoffs and estimates across many projects and trades is better served by STACK or a comparable takeoff platform; someone who needs an instant, private answer to what one driveway, patio, or slab should cost before it is offered is in the right place here.
